modules.title: How Cleaning Products Work, Your Raw Materials and Staying Safe
modules.overview: Before you mix anything, you need to understand what makes a detergent clean, what each chemical in the market does, and how to protect yourself and your family. This module covers surfactants, the common raw materials used in Nigerian liquid soap, and the safety rules for sulphonic acid, caustic soda and bleach.

lessons.title: How detergents clean and which products to start with
objectives: Explain in plain words how a surfactant removes grease
Tell the difference between true soap and a synthetic detergent
Compare common cleaning products by risk and difficulty
Choose a sensible first product for your budget and setting

blocks.text: Every cleaning product on a supermarket shelf, from dishwashing liquid to laundry detergent, depends on one kind of ingredient: a **surfactant**. The word is short for "surface active agent". A surfactant is a molecule with two very different ends. One end, the **head**, loves water. The other end, the **tail**, loves oil and grease and hates water.

blocks.name: bubbles
blocks.caption: Foam and bubbles come from surfactants, the working ingredient in every detergent you will make.

blocks.text: When you wash a greasy pot, the oil-loving tails push into the grease. Thousands of surfactant molecules surround each small drop of oil, with their water-loving heads facing outward. Now the grease is wrapped in a coat that water can hold, so rinsing carries it away. This is why plain water cannot remove palm oil from a plate, but water with detergent can.
Soap and detergent are not the same thing

**True soap** is made by reacting fats or oils with a strong alkali such as caustic soda. Bar soap and traditional black soap are true soaps. **Synthetic detergents** are surfactants made in factories, mostly from petroleum or plant raw materials. In Nigeria, the keg "liquid soap" sold for dishes and general cleaning is almost always a synthetic detergent, made from chemicals such as **sulphonic acid** (linear alkylbenzene sulphonic acid, also called LABSA) and **SLES** (sodium laureth sulphate, often sold as "texapon").

Detergents have one big advantage over soap: they keep working in **hard water**. Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium. These react with soap to form the grey scum you see in some bathrooms, and the soap stops foaming. Synthetic detergents are much less affected, which is one reason they took over laundry and dishwashing.

blocks.title: True soap vs synthetic detergent
items: True soap
Synthetic detergent
blocks.caption: This course focuses on synthetic liquid detergents, the products most households here buy in kegs and bottles.

blocks.text: Course descriptions sometimes promise that you will "make disinfectants". Here we will be honest: in this course you will learn to **use** bleach safely to disinfect, and to understand what a real disinfectant claim requires. You will **make** liquid detergents, which clean by removing dirt and grease. Cleaning removes most germs along with the dirt, but it is not the same as a tested disinfectant, and you must never label it as one.
Why liquid soap is a common first business

items: Every household, restaurant, school, church, mosque, hotel and office uses it, and buys it again and again.
The raw materials are sold in chemical markets in most Nigerian cities, often in small quantities.
A batch can be mixed with plastic drums and stirring paddles, without electricity.
It can be sold in many sizes, from small bottles to 25-litre kegs for bulk buyers.

blocks.text: The same things make the market crowded. Many sellers make thin, watery products to cut cost, or skip safety and labelling. Your advantage will be **consistency and trust**: a product that cleans well, is the same every batch, is safe on hands, and is honestly labelled.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing a first product
blocks.context: For example, Halima lives in Kaduna with her husband and three children. She has about 60,000 naira (approximate) to start, a covered backyard space, and wants to sell to neighbours and two restaurants nearby.
steps: She lists what buyers around her already use: restaurants buy dishwashing liquid in kegs, neighbours buy small bottles of multipurpose liquid soap.
She rules out bleach production and disinfectants because they carry high chemical risk and need regulatory approval she does not yet have.
She chooses multipurpose liquid soap because she can sell it to both groups and the raw materials are available in Kaduna's chemical market.
She decides to mix only in the covered backyard, never in the kitchen, and only when the children are at school.
blocks.result: Halima starts with one product, multipurpose liquid soap, aimed at restaurants (kegs) and neighbours (bottles). She adds liquid hand wash only after she can make the first product well every time.

blocks.title: Cleaning is not the same as disinfecting
blocks.text: A detergent lifts dirt and grease so they can be rinsed away. A disinfectant kills germs on a surface after it has been cleaned. Keep these words separate in how you talk about and label your products.

takeaways: Surfactants have a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail, which lets water carry grease away
Keg liquid soap is usually a synthetic detergent, not true soap
Detergents work better than soap in hard water
Start with multipurpose liquid soap; do not manufacture bleach or disinfectants as a beginner

activity.title: Survey your local cleaning products market
steps: Visit one market, supermarket or roadside seller, or check three WhatsApp sellers near you.
Write down five cleaning products: type, size, price, and whether a NAFDAC number is printed.
Pour a little of any keg liquid soap you can buy cheaply into a clear bottle and note its thickness and colour.
Write three sentences on which product you will make first, who will buy it, and why.
activity.evidence: A photo of your notes or a table of five products with prices, plus your three-sentence decision.

lessons.title: Raw materials: what each chemical does
objectives: Name the common raw materials in Nigerian liquid soap and their jobs
Explain why sulphonic acid must be neutralised before use
Read active matter percentages on a supplier's label
Choose safer alternatives to formalin as a preservative

blocks.text: Walk into a chemical shop and you will hear many names: sulphonic, caustic, soda ash, texapon, nitrosol, STTP, foam booster, formalin. Sellers often use local trade names, and the same chemical can have three names. In this lesson you will learn what each one actually is and **what job it does** in the product. When you understand the job, you can judge any recipe you are given instead of copying it blindly.

blocks.name: test-tube
blocks.caption: Each raw material has one main job; knowing the job helps you judge any formula.

blocks.text: The cleaning agents (surfactants)

**Sulphonic acid** (linear alkylbenzene sulphonic acid, LABSA) is a thick, dark brown, oily liquid. It is the raw form of one of the most widely used detergent surfactants in the world, linear alkylbenzene sulphonate (LAS). It replaced older branched versions because it breaks down more readily in the environment. As bought, it is a **strong, corrosive acid**. It cannot be used on hands or dishes until it is **neutralised** with an alkali, which turns it into its sodium salt, the actual cleaning agent.

**SLES** (sodium laureth sulphate) is usually sold as a thick white or clear paste, often labelled 70%. That number is the **active matter**: 100 g of 70% paste contains about 70 g of actual surfactant and 30 g of water. SLES foams well and is gentler on skin than neutralised sulphonic acid, so it is used in hand wash and added to multipurpose soap. It dissolves slowly; break it up and stir patiently, or soak it in some of the batch water first.

**SLS** (sodium lauryl sulphate) is a related surfactant, usually a powder or needles. It is a strong foamer but harsher on skin than SLES, and its dust irritates the nose and eyes, so wear a dust mask when handling it.
The alkalis and builders

blocks.text: **Foam booster** is a trade name, not one chemical. Ask the seller exactly what it is and request a data sheet. Foam makes buyers happy, but more foam does not mean better cleaning. A product can foam hugely and still leave grease behind.
Colour, perfume and preservative

Use colours and perfumes sold for detergents or cosmetics, not food colour or random oils, because they must stay stable in the product. Add perfume near the end, when the batch has cooled, so the scent is not lost.

A water-based product with thickeners can grow mould and bacteria, especially in a warm climate. That is why it needs a **preservative**. Many local recipes use **formalin**, which is a solution of formaldehyde in water. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies formaldehyde as a human carcinogen. Its vapour also irritates the eyes and lungs. Avoid it. Ask your supplier for a preservative made for detergents or cosmetics, ask for its data sheet and the recommended dose, and follow that dose.

blocks.title: Buy with labels, not just names
blocks.text: Only buy chemicals in containers with a clear label showing the chemical name and, where possible, the strength. Ask for the safety data sheet (SDS). If a seller cannot tell you what is in "foam booster" or "special thickener", do not put it in a product people use on their hands and plates.

blocks.title: What makes a liquid soap work
items: Perfume, colour, preservative
Thickener and salt
Builders: soda ash, STPP
Surfactants: LAS and SLES
blocks.caption: The surfactants at the base do the cleaning; everything above supports them, so never cut the base to save money.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading active matter
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Onitsha compares two SLES pastes. Seller A sells a 70% paste. Seller B sells a cheaper paste but cannot say its strength.
steps: She works out that 1,000 g of Seller A's paste gives about 700 g of active surfactant (1,000 x 0.70).
She asks Seller B for a label or data sheet. He has none.
She knows that if B's paste were only 50% active, 1,000 g would give 500 g of surfactant, so her product would be weaker even if it looked the same.
She chooses Seller A and writes the supplier, strength and batch number in her records.
blocks.result: Ifeoma buys on known strength, not just price. Her product stays consistent because the amount of real cleaning agent in each batch is the same.

blocks.title: Store raw materials properly
blocks.text: Keep lids tight: caustic soda absorbs moisture from air and becomes hard and lumpy, and sulphonic acid gives off fumes. Store acids and alkalis on separate shelves, off the floor, away from sunlight, children and food.

takeaways: Sulphonic acid is a corrosive acid that becomes a cleaning agent only after neutralisation
SLES strength is shown as active matter, for example 70%
Soda ash and STPP help in hard water; nitrosol, CMC and salt thicken
Avoid formalin; use a supplier's detergent preservative at its stated dose
Always buy labelled chemicals and ask for the safety data sheet

activity.title: Build your raw materials sheet
steps: Visit or call one chemical seller and ask the price, pack size and strength of sulphonic acid, caustic soda, soda ash, SLES and nitrosol.
Ask for a safety data sheet for sulphonic acid and caustic soda, or find one online for the product name on the label.
Make a table with columns: local name, chemical name, job, strength, pack size, approximate price, seller.
Mark any item whose real chemical name or strength you could not confirm.
activity.evidence: Your completed raw materials table (photo or file) with at least five items.

lessons.title: Chemical safety: PPE, workspace, bleach rules and first aid
objectives: Set up a safe mixing area with the right protective equipment
State the safe order for diluting caustic soda and sulphonic acid
Explain why bleach must never meet acids or ammonia
Give correct first aid for chemical splashes and fumes

blocks.text: Sulphonic acid and caustic soda are both **corrosive**: they can burn skin and cause permanent eye damage within seconds. Bleach can release dangerous gas when mixed with the wrong product. None of this means you should be afraid. It means you work with a routine, every single time, so that a mistake is unlikely and a splash is harmless.

blocks.name: goggles
blocks.caption: Splash goggles are the most important item you will buy for this business.

blocks.text: Personal protective equipment (PPE)

items: **Chemical splash goggles** that seal around the eyes. Ordinary glasses leave gaps at the sides.
**Rubber or nitrile gloves**, long enough to cover the wrists. Replace them if torn.
**Long sleeves, long trousers or wrapper, an apron, and closed shoes.** No slippers.
**A dust mask** when weighing powders such as caustic soda, soda ash, STPP or SLS.
Tie back long hair and remove loose jewellery.

blocks.text: Your workspace

items: Mix outdoors under a shade or in a room with open windows and moving air, never in the kitchen where you cook.
Keep children and animals away while chemicals are out. A locked area is best.
Use plastic drums and buckets (HDPE or PP) or stainless steel. Never use **aluminium**: caustic soda attacks it and gives off hydrogen gas, which can catch fire.
Keep a large container of clean water within reach for rinsing splashes.
Never store chemicals or finished products in drink bottles. Children have been poisoned this way.

blocks.text: Safe mixing order

items: Caustic soda: measure cold water first, then add the caustic soda slowly to the water while stirring. Never pour water onto caustic soda: it can boil up and splash.
The caustic solution gets very hot. Let it cool before adding it to anything else.
Sulphonic acid: pour it slowly into the water or batch, never the other way round, stirring as you go.
Neutralising acid with alkali gives off heat. Add the alkali in small portions and stir between additions.
Soda ash fizzes when it meets acid (it releases carbon dioxide). Add it slowly so the batch does not foam over.

blocks.text: Bleach: the rule with no exceptions

Household bleach contains **sodium hypochlorite**. Mixed with **acids** (such as many toilet cleaners, vinegar, or sulphonic acid), it releases **chlorine gas**. Mixed with **ammonia** (found in some glass cleaners and in urine), it releases **chloramine gases**. Both cause coughing, chest pain, breathing difficulty and watery eyes, and higher exposures can damage the lungs and kill. The US CDC advises never mixing household bleach with any other cleaners or disinfectants.

items: Never add bleach to your liquid soap batch or to any product you make.
Never put bleach into a container that once held sulphonic acid or an acidic toilet cleaner.
Tell customers clearly: use bleach on its own, rinse the surface, then use other cleaners.

blocks.title: Before every batch
items: Goggles, gloves, sleeves on
Children and animals away
Rinse water within reach
No aluminium, no bleach nearby
Containers labelled
blocks.caption: Run this check every time, even for a small test batch.

blocks.text: First aid

head: What happened
What to do
rows: Splash in the eye
Rinse immediately with clean running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open. Go to a hospital straight after.
Splash on skin
Remove contaminated clothing. Rinse with plenty of running water for at least 15 minutes. Seek medical care if the skin is red, painful or broken.
Breathed fumes or gas (for example bleach mixed with acid)
Leave the area at once into fresh air. Get medical help if coughing, chest pain or breathing difficulty continues.
Swallowed
Do not make the person vomit. Rinse the mouth with water and go to a hospital immediately, taking the container.

blocks.title: No vinegar on burns
blocks.text: Do not try to neutralise a caustic burn with vinegar or an acid burn with soda. The reaction gives off heat and wastes time. Plenty of running water is the correct first aid for both.

**Spills.** If you spill caustic soda solution or sulphonic acid, keep people away, put on your PPE, and soak up the liquid with sand, sawdust or old cloths. Scoop it into a labelled plastic container. Then wash the area with plenty of water. Do not try to neutralise a large spill by pouring the other chemical on it, because the reaction gives off heat and can splash. Never wash concentrated chemicals into a well, borehole area or open gutter.

blocks.title: Worked example: a near miss handled well
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Ibadan is pouring caustic soda solution into her batch when some splashes onto her forearm, just above her glove.
steps: She puts the jug down safely and goes straight to the bucket of rinse water she placed nearby.
She rinses her arm under running water from a jug and a tap for at least 15 minutes.
The skin is red but not broken; she watches it and plans to see a clinic if it blisters.
In her batch record she writes what happened and changes her routine: longer gloves and long sleeves taped at the cuff.
blocks.result: Because the water was ready and Grace knew the rule, the splash caused only mild redness. Her written fix prevents the same accident next time.

takeaways: Splash goggles, gloves, long sleeves and closed shoes every time
Add caustic soda to water and acid to water, slowly, never the reverse
Bleach plus acid gives chlorine gas; bleach plus ammonia gives chloramine gas
First aid for splashes is running water for at least 15 minutes, then medical care
Never use aluminium or drink bottles

activity.title: Set up and photograph your safety station
steps: Choose your mixing area and remove food, cooking items and anything aluminium.
Gather goggles, gloves, apron, dust mask and a filled rinse-water container.
Write a one-page safety card: mixing order, the bleach rule, and first aid, and stick it on the wall.
Write the nearest hospital or clinic and an emergency phone number on the card.
Ask a family member to read the card and explain the bleach rule back to you.
activity.evidence: Photos of your safety station and your safety card on the wall.

quiz.q: Why can water with detergent remove palm oil from a plate when plain water cannot?
options: Surfactant tails grab the oil and heads let water carry it away
quiz.explain: Each surfactant molecule has an oil-loving tail and a water-loving head, so grease gets wrapped and rinsed away.

quiz.q: Ada wants to start a cleaning products business next month with little money. Which first product is most sensible?
quiz.explain: Multipurpose liquid soap uses a well-known method and simple equipment. Bleach and disinfectants carry high risk and need approval.

quiz.q: Why must sulphonic acid be neutralised before the product is used?
options: As bought, it is a strong corrosive acid
It will not foam until it is heated
It is too thin to sell
quiz.explain: Sulphonic acid only becomes a skin-safe cleaning agent after it reacts with an alkali such as caustic soda or soda ash.

quiz.q: A seller offers a cheap SLES paste but cannot say its strength. What is the main risk?
options: It may contain less active surfactant, so the product is weaker
quiz.explain: Active matter tells you how much real surfactant you get. Unknown strength means inconsistent, possibly weak products.

quiz.q: Bisi's customer says she mixes bleach with an acidic toilet cleaner to make it "stronger". What should Bisi tell her?
options: That is fine if the room is open
Stop: this releases chlorine gas, which can seriously harm breathing
Use warm water instead of cold
quiz.explain: Bleach and acids release chlorine gas. Bleach must be used on its own.

quiz.q: Caustic soda solution splashes into Kemi's eye. What should happen first?
options: Rinse with clean running water for at least 15 minutes, then go to hospital
Rub the eye with a dry cloth
Put a few drops of vinegar in the eye
Wait 10 minutes to see if it hurts
quiz.explain: Immediate, prolonged rinsing with water is the correct first aid, followed by urgent medical care.

modules.title: Making Your First Batches: Liquid Soap, Test Batches and Hand Wash
modules.overview: Now you make real product. You will follow the standard method for multipurpose liquid soap, learn to run small test batches and scale them up with simple arithmetic, and make a milder hand wash. You will also learn to disinfect with bleach safely and what a genuine disinfectant claim requires.

lessons.title: Multipurpose liquid soap, step by step
objectives: Prepare the thickener, acid and alkali stages in the right order
Neutralise sulphonic acid by checking pH with test strips
Thicken, colour, perfume and preserve a batch
Rest, bottle and record a finished batch

blocks.text: Most Nigerian multipurpose liquid soap is made by the same basic method, even though every trainer's quantities differ. In this lesson you learn the **method and the reason for each stage**. For quantities, start from a formula sheet you trust (for example from a trainer you have watched work, or a supplier's starter formula), then prove it with a small test batch as you will learn in the next lesson. Do not trust a formula only because it is popular on social media.

blocks.name: bucket
blocks.caption: Liquid soap is mixed in plastic drums and buckets with a clean stirring paddle, no electricity needed.

blocks.text: Equipment

items: Plastic drums or buckets (HDPE or PP) with lids, sized for your batch plus room to stir.
A long plastic or wooden stirring paddle used only for soap making.
A digital scale for powders and a measuring jug for liquids.
Universal pH test strips (they cover pH 1 to 14).
Your full PPE and rinse water, as set up in Module 1.

blocks.title: Liquid soap production stages
items: Hydrate thickener in water
Stir in sulphonic acid
Neutralise, check pH
Add SLES, builders
Thicken, perfume, preserve
Rest, then bottle
blocks.caption: Each stage must be finished before the next begins, which is why order matters more than speed.

blocks.text: The stages explained

items: **Prepare the thickener.** Sprinkle nitrosol (HEC) slowly onto the measured water while stirring, so each grain gets wet separately. If you dump it in, it forms lumps that never dissolve. Many makers leave it to swell for several hours or overnight until the water is clear and thick.

**Dissolve the alkalis separately.** In a separate plastic container, add caustic soda slowly to cold water and let it cool. Dissolve soda ash in water in another container. Keep STPP dissolved separately as well if your formula uses it.
**Add the sulphonic acid.** Pour the sulphonic acid slowly into the thickened water, stirring steadily in one direction. The mix will turn darker and may smell sharp; keep your face back.

**Neutralise slowly.** Add the caustic solution and soda ash solution in small portions, stirring well after each. Soda ash will fizz. The batch will warm up. After each portion, dip a pH strip into a small sample and compare the colour.
**Stop at the right pH.** Aim for close to neutral, around pH 7. Below about 6 means acid remains and the soap will sting hands. Well above 9 means too much alkali, which is harsh on skin.
**Add SLES and builders.** Stir in the SLES (pre-soaked in some batch water helps) and any STPP solution until smooth.

**Adjust thickness, then finish.** If needed, add salt dissolved in water a little at a time (see the next lesson for why). When the batch has cooled, add colour, perfume and preservative at the doses given on their data sheets.
**Rest.** Cover and leave the batch for 12 to 24 hours so foam settles and air bubbles rise. Check pH again, then bottle.

blocks.title: Why pH is measured, not guessed
blocks.text: Sulphonic acid strength and caustic soda purity vary between suppliers and even between drums. A fixed amount of caustic that was right for one drum can leave another batch acidic or too alkaline. Always neutralise in portions and check with pH strips. This is the single most important quality step.

blocks.title: Worked example: correcting the pH during neutralisation
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Enugu is making a 20-litre batch using a formula from her trainer. Her sulphonic acid is from a new supplier.
steps: After adding the caustic and soda ash amounts on her sheet, she tests a sample: the strip shows about pH 5.
She knows this means acid is still present, so she does not continue to the SLES stage.
She dissolves a little extra soda ash in water and adds it in two small portions, stirring and testing after each.
After the second portion the strip shows about pH 7. She records the extra amount and the supplier's name in her batch record.
blocks.result: The batch is neutral and safe on hands. Ngozi now knows the new supplier's acid needs a little more alkali, and she will check this again with her next drum.

blocks.text: Bottling

Use clean bottles or kegs with tight caps. Rinse them with clean water and let them drain dry. Never reuse containers that held chemicals, food oil or drinks. Fill to the same level every time, cap tightly, and write the **batch number** on each container or on the label before it leaves your workspace.

blocks.title: Clean as you go
blocks.text: Wash the drum, paddle and jugs with plenty of water as soon as a batch is bottled, while wearing gloves. Dried product and acid residue can contaminate the next batch, and a dirty drum can introduce mould. Keep one paddle and one set of jugs only for soap making, never for food.

Expect your first few batches to look slightly different from a factory product. Colour can vary with the shade of the sulphonic acid, and the batch may look cloudy while foam is still settling. What matters is that the pH is right, the thickness is what you planned, and it cleans well. Those three things are what buyers notice after the first purchase.

takeaways: Hydrate nitrosol slowly to avoid lumps
Add sulphonic acid to the batch slowly, then neutralise in small portions
Measure pH after each portion and aim for close to neutral
Add perfume, colour and preservative when the batch has cooled
Rest the batch, check pH again, then bottle with a batch number

activity.title: Write your production card
steps: Copy the eight stages onto a card in your own words, with your PPE reminder at the top.
Next to each stage, write what you will check before moving on (for example: no lumps, pH reading).
Practise the neutralisation step with your pH strips on a sample of any keg soap you bought earlier and record its pH.
Keep the card with your equipment.
activity.evidence: A photo of your production card and a photo of a pH strip result beside the sample you tested.

lessons.title: Test batches, scaling up and the salt curve
objectives: Scale a tested formula down to a small test batch and back up
Calculate active surfactant in a batch from paste strength
Thicken an SLES product with salt without overshooting
Decide whether a test batch is ready to scale

blocks.text: Making a full 25-litre batch on your first try is how money gets wasted. Professional formulators work in **small test batches**, change one thing at a time, and only scale up what works. You can do the same with a kitchen scale, a measuring jug and two-litre containers.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A person using a large calculator
blocks.caption: Simple multiplication and division let you test small and produce big with the same result.

blocks.text: Scaling: the one-litre method

Write every ingredient in your formula **per one litre** of finished product. Then any batch size is a single multiplication. To get the per-litre amount, divide each quantity by the batch size the formula was written for.

blocks.title: Worked example: scaling a formula sheet
blocks.context: For example, Halima's trainer gave her a tested 20-litre formula. One line says 100 ml of perfume. She wants a 2-litre test batch first, then a 25-litre production batch. (These numbers are only to show the arithmetic, not a recipe to copy.)
steps: Per litre: 100 ml divided by 20 L = 5 ml of perfume per litre.
Test batch: 5 ml x 2 L = 10 ml of perfume.
Production batch: 5 ml x 25 L = 125 ml of perfume.
She does the same division and multiplication for every line, writes the results in a table, and double-checks each with her phone calculator.
blocks.result: Halima has one table with three columns (per litre, 2 L, 25 L). Every batch size uses the same proportions, so the test batch truly predicts the big batch.

blocks.text: Active matter: how strong is your product?

Two products can look identical but contain very different amounts of cleaning agent. To compare, work out the **active surfactant** in each batch. Multiply the weight of each surfactant raw material by its strength. For example, 1,500 g of 70% SLES paste gives 1,500 x 0.70 = 1,050 g of active SLES. Dividing the total active weight by the batch weight gives the active percentage, which you can use to keep every batch the same and to compare formulas honestly.
The salt curve

Salt thickens products that contain SLES, but only up to a point. As you add salt, the liquid gets thicker and thicker, reaches a peak, and then **gets thinner again** if you keep adding. Makers call this the salt curve. Once you pass the peak you cannot take the salt out; you can only add more of the other ingredients to dilute it.

blocks.title: Thickening with salt safely
items: Dissolve salt in water
Add a small portion
Stir, wait, check flow
Thicker? Repeat once
Thinner? Stop, note amount
blocks.caption: Small salt portions with checks in between keep you on the rising side of the salt curve.

blocks.text: A simple way to judge thickness is a **flow test**. Fill a clean plastic cup with a small hole in the base, or an empty syringe with the needle removed, and time how many seconds the product takes to run out. Use the same cup every time. Record the seconds in your batch record. Now "thick" becomes a number you can repeat.
What to change, and how

head: Test batch result
Likely cause
Change for the next test
rows: Too thin
Not enough thickener or salt, or past the salt peak
Try a little more nitrosol, or test salt in smaller steps
Lumps or jelly pieces
Nitrosol added too fast or not left to swell
Sprinkle slowly and allow longer to hydrate
Stings hands, pH below 6
Acid not fully neutralised
Add alkali in portions until near pH 7
Slippery, harsh, pH above 9
Too much caustic or soda ash
Reduce alkali; neutralise in smaller steps
Weak on grease
Too little active surfactant
Check your active matter calculation and raw material strength

blocks.title: Change only one thing at a time
blocks.text: If you change the salt, perfume and SLES all at once and the batch improves, you will not know which change worked. Label test containers A, B, C and change a single ingredient in each.
A simple, fair grease test

To compare batches, you need the same test each time. Smear one teaspoon of palm oil on each of two identical plates. Mix the same small amount of each product, for example one teaspoon, into the same volume of water in two bowls. Wash each plate with a clean sponge for the same number of strokes, rinse, and look and feel for oil left behind. You can also count how many greasy plates one measured amount of product washes before the foam disappears. Write the results down. This is how you prove to yourself, and later to buyers, that your product works.

A test batch is ready to scale when it passes all your checks two times in a row: pH near neutral, the flow time you want, no lumps, good grease removal on an oily plate, and no separation after standing for a few days. Write the final per-litre formula clearly and treat it as your **master formula**.

takeaways: Test in small batches and change one thing at a time
Write every formula per litre, then multiply for any batch size
Active surfactant = weight of raw material x its strength
Salt thickens SLES products up to a peak, then thins them
A flow test turns thickness into a repeatable number

activity.title: Make and compare two test batches
steps: Convert your chosen formula into a per-litre table, then into a 1-litre or 2-litre test batch.
Make test batch A exactly as written, with full PPE.
Make test batch B with one change only (for example, a smaller salt amount added in portions).
Record pH, flow time, appearance and a grease test on an oily plate for both batches.
Write which batch you will repeat and why.
activity.evidence: Your per-litre table, the A and B test records, and a photo of both batches side by side.

lessons.title: Liquid hand wash, safe bleach use and disinfectant claims
objectives: Explain why hand wash is usually made mainly from SLES
Dilute household bleach for disinfecting according to recognised guidance
Tell the difference between a cleaner and a disinfectant claim
Decide which products you should and should not make or label

blocks.text: Once your multipurpose liquid soap is consistent, a **liquid hand wash** is a natural second product. It is used many times a day on bare skin, so it must be milder, nicely perfumed and well preserved. This lesson also covers the other thing every cleaning business gets asked about: "Can you make something that kills germs?"

blocks.name: wash-hands
blocks.alt: A person washing hands at a sink
blocks.caption: Hand wash touches skin many times a day, so mildness and correct pH matter more than foam.

blocks.text: What makes hand wash different

items: It is usually based mainly on **SLES**, which is gentler on skin than neutralised sulphonic acid.
Many makers add a milder co-surfactant such as **cocamidopropyl betaine** (often called CAPB) to make it softer on hands; ask your supplier for it by name and for its data sheet.
**Glycerine** helps hands feel less dry after washing.
It is thickened mainly with salt (watch the salt curve) and should be close to neutral pH.
Because people dip into it daily, a **preservative** at the supplier's stated dose is essential.
Weigh the SLES and break it into pieces in part of the water; stir gently until fully dissolved. Stirring too hard creates foam that takes hours to settle.
Add the remaining water, the co-surfactant if used, and glycerine; stir gently.
Check pH. Adjust only in very small steps if needed, following your tested formula.
Thicken with salt solution in small portions and use your flow test.
Add perfume, colour and preservative; rest for 12 to 24 hours; check again and bottle in pump bottles.

blocks.text: Before you sell a hand wash, use it yourself several times a day for a week, and ask two or three adults to do the same. Ask them specific questions: does it leave hands tight or dry, is the scent too strong, does the pump dispense easily? Anyone who gets redness or itching should stop using it at once. A milder formula and a lower perfume dose are the usual fixes.
Disinfecting with bleach, safely

For killing germs on hard surfaces at home, household bleach is effective and cheap, so your customers do not need you to invent a disinfectant. Teach them to use it correctly. The US CDC gives this guidance for household bleach containing **5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite**:

items: Clean the surface with detergent and water first, because dirt protects germs.
Mix 5 tablespoons (one third of a cup) of bleach per gallon of room-temperature water, or 4 teaspoons per quart. That works out to roughly 20 ml of bleach per litre of water.
Leave it on the surface for at least 1 minute before wiping.
Make a fresh solution every day; it loses strength after 24 hours.
Never mix bleach with any other cleaner or disinfectant.

blocks.title: Check the strength on your bottle
blocks.text: Bleach brands sold in Nigeria differ in strength, and some are weaker than 5%. The CDC amounts above are for 5% to 9% bleach. Read the label and follow the manufacturer's dilution directions for disinfecting. If the label gives no strength, follow its directions exactly.

Store bleach in its original opaque bottle with the cap tight, in a cool place away from sunlight, because heat and light make it lose strength. Keep it away from acids, including toilet cleaners and sulphonic acid. Any diluted bleach solution should go in a clearly labelled container, never a drink bottle, and should be thrown away at the end of the day. Bleach also removes colour from clothes and can damage some metals, so warn customers to keep it off fabrics and to rinse metal surfaces after use.

blocks.title: Cleaner vs disinfectant
items: Cleaner (what you make)
Disinfectant (registered product)
blocks.caption: If your label promises to kill germs, you are selling a disinfectant and must be able to prove it.

blocks.text: Why not make bleach or disinfectants yet?

Some trainers teach making bleach from chlorine chemicals such as calcium hypochlorite, sold as HTH. This involves strong oxidising chemicals and a risk of releasing chlorine gas, and home-made bleach can lose strength quickly in storage, so the customer cannot know how strong it is. Germ-killing products are also checked carefully by regulators. NAFDAC's list of products allowed under its micro-scale scheme includes laundry detergents, soaps and liquid air fresheners, but it does not list disinfectants or bleach. Ask NAFDAC directly before you plan any germ-killing product.

blocks.title: Worked example: answering a customer honestly
blocks.context: For example, a restaurant owner asks Grace, who sells liquid soap in Ibadan, for "liquid soap that kills 99.9% of germs".
steps: Grace explains that her liquid soap is a cleaner: it removes grease and dirt, which is the first step of hygiene.
She explains that killing germs is a separate step, and recommends a registered bleach diluted according to its label, after washing.
She shows the owner how to make a fresh bleach solution each morning in a labelled container, and to never mix it with the liquid soap or toilet cleaner.
She keeps her own label honest: "multipurpose liquid soap, cuts grease", with no germ claims.
blocks.result: The restaurant gets a safe, correct routine, Grace keeps the order for liquid soap, and she avoids an illegal claim she could not prove.

takeaways: Hand wash is usually SLES-based, near neutral and always preserved
Stir SLES gently to avoid foam
CDC guidance: for 5% to 9% bleach, about 20 ml per litre, fresh daily, at least 1 minute contact
Never claim your detergent kills germs; that makes it a disinfectant
Do not manufacture bleach or disinfectants as a beginner

activity.title: Make a hand wash test batch and a bleach guide card
steps: Make a 1-litre hand wash test batch from a tested formula, wearing PPE.
Record pH, flow time and how it feels after washing hands three times.
Read the label of one bleach brand in your area and write down its stated strength and dilution directions.
Write a short customer card: how to dilute that bleach, contact time, make fresh daily, never mix.
activity.evidence: Hand wash test record, a photo of the bleach label, and your customer bleach card.

quiz.q: Chika poured nitrosol into her drum all at once and now has lumps that will not dissolve. What should she do next time?
options: Sprinkle it slowly while stirring and let it swell
Heat the drum on a fire
quiz.explain: Nitrosol must be sprinkled slowly so each grain wets separately, then left to hydrate.

quiz.q: After neutralising, Amina's sample shows pH 5. What does this mean?
options: Acid remains; add alkali in small portions and test again
quiz.explain: Below about pH 6 means unneutralised acid. Add alkali gradually until close to pH 7.

quiz.q: A 20-litre formula uses 100 ml of perfume. How much is needed for a 25-litre batch?
quiz.explain: 100 / 20 = 5 ml per litre. 5 x 25 = 125 ml.

quiz.q: Funke keeps adding salt to thicken her hand wash, but it has started getting thinner. Why?
options: She passed the peak of the salt curve
SLES does not react to salt
quiz.explain: Salt thickens SLES products up to a peak; beyond it the product thins again.

quiz.q: How much active SLES is in 2,000 g of 70% SLES paste?
quiz.explain: 2,000 x 0.70 = 1,400 g of active SLES.

quiz.q: A buyer wants Rose to print "kills 99.9% of germs" on her liquid soap. What is the right response?
options: Print it; most brands say it
Decline: a germ-kill claim makes it a disinfectant that needs proof and approval
Add bleach to the soap to make it true
quiz.explain: Germ-killing claims require tested evidence and regulatory approval. Adding bleach to products is dangerous.

modules.title: Quality, Honest Labelling, NAFDAC and Responsible Production
modules.overview: A product that is good one week and watery the next will lose customers. This module gives you a simple quality testing routine, a fault-fixing guide, the contents of an honest label, the basic NAFDAC registration path for small producers, and the records and waste rules that keep your business safe and trusted.

lessons.title: Quality tests and fixing common faults
objectives: Run five simple quality tests on every batch
Diagnose common faults such as separation, cloudiness and stinging
Decide whether a batch can be sold, reworked or discarded
Set your own written product specification

blocks.text: Big manufacturers test every batch against a **specification**: a short list of measurements the product must meet before it is released. You can do the same with tools that cost very little. Your specification is your promise to customers that the bottle they buy next month will be the same as the one they liked today.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.caption: A written specification and a test record turn quality from a feeling into a habit.

blocks.text: Five tests for every batch

head: Test
How to do it
What you record
rows: pH
Dip a universal pH strip into a small sample and compare the colour after the time stated on the pack
pH reading, for example 7
Thickness
Flow test with the same cup or syringe every time
Seconds to empty
Appearance and smell
Look at a sample in a clear bottle against light; smell it
Clear or cloudy, colour, any lumps, scent strength
Cleaning
Grease test on oily plates, same method each time
Pass or fail, plates washed per measured amount
Stability
Keep a sealed sample bottle on a shelf for at least a week and look at it daily
Any separation, layers, mould, colour change or smell change

blocks.text: Keep a **retained sample** from every batch: a small sealed bottle labelled with the batch number and date. If a customer complains later, you can look at the same batch and see whether the problem was in the product or in how it was stored or used.
Common faults and fixes

head: Fault
Likely cause
What to do
rows: Stings or burns hands
pH too low (acid left) or too high (excess alkali)
Do not sell. Check pH and correct in small steps, then retest
Separates into layers
Not enough thickener, too much salt, or poor mixing
Stir well and retest; for the next batch review thickener and salt amounts
Cloudy or gritty
Undissolved soda ash, STPP or salt, or foam not settled
Let it rest longer; dissolve powders fully in water before adding next time
Lumps or jelly pieces
Nitrosol added too fast
Strain if possible; next time sprinkle slowly and hydrate longer
Watery, little cleaning
Too little active surfactant, or past the salt peak
Check the active matter calculation and the raw material strength
Mould, bad smell after weeks
No preservative, too little, or dirty containers
Discard. Use a proper preservative at its dose and clean containers
Colour fades
Unsuitable dye or sunlight
Use detergent-grade colour; store away from sunlight

blocks.title: The quality loop
items: Test against specification
Find the cause
Fix one thing
Retest and record
Update master formula
blocks.caption: Every fault you solve and write down makes the next batch more reliable.

blocks.text: Sell, rework or discard?

items: **Sell** only when the batch meets every line of your specification.
**Rework** when the fix is safe and simple, such as adjusting pH or thickness, then test again fully.
**Discard** when there is mould, a bad smell, unknown contamination, or you cannot find the cause. Never sell a doubtful batch at a discount; a cheap bad product still carries your name.

blocks.title: Worked example: writing a specification
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Onitsha has made four good test batches of her multipurpose liquid soap and wants a written specification.
steps: She looks at her four records: pH readings were 7, 7, 7 and 8; flow times were 22, 25, 24 and 23 seconds in her syringe test.
She writes: pH 7 to 8; flow time 20 to 26 seconds; clear green, no lumps; passes the grease test; no separation after 7 days.
Her fifth production batch reads pH 7 but flows in 14 seconds, outside her range.
She adds salt solution in small portions, testing after each, until the flow time is 21 seconds, then records the change.
blocks.result: Ifeoma's specification lets her catch a thin batch before it reaches customers, and her record shows exactly what she did to fix it.

blocks.text: Shelf life and expiry dates

Your label needs a best-before or expiry date, and that date should come from evidence, not guesswork. Keep retained samples from your first batches and check them every week for a few months: look for separation, mould, colour change, a sour or musty smell, and changes in thickness and pH. If a sample is still good after three months, you have evidence for a three-month date. Extend the date only as your samples prove it. Products stored in hot shops or in sunlight age faster, so tell resellers to keep them in the shade.

blocks.title: Read pH strips correctly
blocks.text: Use a clean, dry spoon or stick to take a sample, dip the strip briefly, and compare the colour at the time printed on the pack, in daylight. Keep the strip pack tightly closed and dry, because damp strips give wrong readings. Record the number, not just "okay".

blocks.title: Foam is not a quality test
blocks.text: Buyers love foam, but foam alone does not show cleaning power or safety. Use foam only as a feature to describe, and rely on pH, thickness, grease removal and stability to judge quality.

takeaways: Test pH, thickness, appearance, cleaning and stability on every batch
Keep a labelled retained sample from each batch
Fix one cause at a time and retest
Discard batches with mould, bad smell or unknown problems
Write a specification from your own good batches

activity.title: Test a batch and write your specification
steps: Run all five tests on your latest test batch and record the results.
Keep a retained sample bottle with batch number and date.
From your best batches so far, write a draft specification with a range for pH and flow time.
Check your retained sample every day for seven days and note any change.
activity.evidence: Test record sheet, photo of your labelled retained sample, and your written specification.

lessons.title: Honest labels, safety warnings and NAFDAC basics
objectives: List what a household cleaning product label should show
Write safety warnings and directions customers will follow
Avoid claims you cannot prove
Outline NAFDAC's micro-scale registration path

blocks.text: A label does three jobs. It tells the buyer **what the product is and how to use it safely**. It tells the buyer **who made it**, so she can come back or complain. And it shows regulators and big buyers that you are a serious producer. In Nigeria, the **National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)** regulates detergents and other household chemical products, along with food, drugs and cosmetics.

blocks.name: label
blocks.caption: An honest, complete label is part of the product, not decoration.

blocks.text: What to put on your label

items: Product name and what it is, for example "Multipurpose liquid soap".
Your brand name, business name and address or phone number.
Net contents, for example 1 litre or 4 litres.
Main ingredients, for example "water, sodium alkylbenzene sulphonate, sodium laureth sulphate, salt, thickener, preservative, colour, fragrance".
Directions for use, for example how much to use per bowl of water.
Safety warnings (see below).
Batch number and production date, and a best-before or expiry date based on your stability checks.
Your NAFDAC registration number, once you have one. Never print a number you have not been given.

blocks.text: Check NAFDAC's current labelling requirements before printing a large stock of labels, because requirements are updated from time to time. Start with a small print run or stickers.
Safety warnings customers will read

items: Keep out of reach of children.
Avoid contact with eyes. If it gets in the eyes, rinse with plenty of water.
If swallowed, do not induce vomiting; seek medical advice and show this label.
Do not mix with bleach or other cleaning products.
Store in the original container with the cap closed. Do not transfer into drink bottles.

blocks.text: Claims: what you can and cannot say

head: Acceptable (if true)
Do not say
rows: Cuts grease on pots and plates
Kills 99.9% of germs (a disinfectant claim)
Lemon fragrance
Antibacterial or antiseptic (unless registered as such)
Works in hard water
100% natural or chemical free (it is made of chemicals, like everything)
Gentle formula, near neutral pH (if tested)
Safe for babies or doctor recommended (without proof)

blocks.text: NAFDAC basics for small producers

NAFDAC runs a scheme for **Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs)**. Its MSME page lists products allowed under the micro and small scheme, including **laundry detergents, soaps and liquid air fresheners**. The main points it states for micro scale are:

items: A micro-scale facility has **not more than nine employees**.
**Not more than five products** can be registered under micro scale.

Documents listed include evidence of **CAC registration** (Corporate Affairs Commission), a site use agreement, trademark approval, one vetting sample and three labels, a fumigation certificate and a payment receipt.
The page lists a micro-scale cosmetic fee (41,000 naira at the time of writing). Fees change, so confirm the current amount with NAFDAC before you budget.
The listing certificate is valid for **two years**.

blocks.title: Path to a NAFDAC listing
items: Stable formula and records
Register business name with CAC
Clean site and labels ready
Apply through NAFDAC
Inspection and sample review
Listing number on labels
blocks.caption: Prepare your formula, records and site first, so the application is not your first contact with good practice.

blocks.title: Beware of fake shortcuts
blocks.text: Pay only through official NAFDAC channels and confirm requirements on nafdac.gov.ng or at a NAFDAC office. Be careful of anyone offering to "get you a number in a few days". A fake or borrowed number can lead to seizure of goods and prosecution.
Directions people can follow

Directions should be short, specific and easy to follow. For a multipurpose liquid soap, tell the buyer how much to use for a bowl of washing-up water, how to use it on floors or surfaces, and to rinse well after use. For hand wash, say to apply to wet hands, lather, and rinse. Test your own directions: if one teaspoon in a bowl washes ten oily plates in your grease test, say so. Clear directions also help customers use less product, which makes them trust that your product is concentrated and worth its price.

When NAFDAC inspects a small production site, officers look at whether the place is clean and organised, whether raw materials and finished goods are stored properly, whether workers use protective equipment, and whether you keep records. The habits in this course, a safety station, labelled containers, batch records and retained samples, are exactly the kind of good practice that makes an inspection easier.

blocks.title: Worked example: fixing a label
blocks.context: For example, Halima's first label in Kaduna says: "Super Clean Liquid Soap. Kills all germs. 100% safe." and nothing else.
steps: She removes "Kills all germs" because it is a disinfectant claim she cannot prove.
She replaces "100% safe" with real safety warnings, including "Do not mix with bleach".
She adds net contents (1 litre), main ingredients, directions, her phone number, batch number and production date.
She plans her CAC business name registration as the first step toward a NAFDAC listing.
blocks.result: Halima's new label is honest and useful, protects customers, and puts her on the path to registration instead of risking her business on false claims.

takeaways: NAFDAC regulates detergents and household chemical products in Nigeria
Labels need name, maker, contents, ingredients, directions, warnings and batch number
Never claim germ killing or "chemical free"
NAFDAC's micro scheme lists laundry detergents and soaps; up to five products and up to nine employees
Confirm current fees and requirements directly with NAFDAC

activity.title: Draft your label and NAFDAC readiness list
steps: Write a full draft label for your main product using the list in this lesson.
Check every claim against the table and remove anything you cannot prove.
Visit nafdac.gov.ng (MSME page) or a NAFDAC office and note the current requirements and fees.
Make a readiness checklist: CAC registration, site, labels, records, samples, with a date for each.
activity.evidence: Your draft label (photo or file) and dated NAFDAC readiness checklist.

lessons.title: Batch records, safe storage and responsible waste
objectives: Keep a batch record that lets you trace any bottle back to its raw materials
Store raw materials and finished products safely
Dispose of chemical waste and rinse water responsibly
Make fair, safe choices that protect customers and neighbours

blocks.text: Records are what turn a kitchen experiment into a business. When a customer says "the last keg was too thin", a batch record tells you exactly what went into that keg, who supplied it, and what the tests showed. Good records also show NAFDAC inspectors and large buyers that you work carefully.

blocks.name: spreadsheet
blocks.alt: A person working on a spreadsheet
blocks.caption: A simple batch record in a notebook or spreadsheet lets you trace every bottle back to its ingredients.

blocks.text: What goes in a batch record

items: Batch number, for example LS-2611-03 (product, year and month, batch of the month).
Date, batch size, and who made it.
Each raw material: name, supplier, strength, and the amount actually used.
Any extra alkali or salt added during adjustments, and why.
Test results: pH, flow time, appearance, grease test, and stability check after a week.
Number of bottles or kegs filled, and the decision: released, reworked or discarded.
Any safety incident or near miss, and the fix.

blocks.title: Worked example: tracing a complaint
blocks.context: For example, a school bursar in Abuja tells Amaka that the last two kegs of her liquid soap stung the cleaners' hands.
steps: Amaka reads the batch number on the kegs: LS-2610-04.
Her record shows that batch used a new drum of sulphonic acid and was bottled with pH 6, which is below her specification of 7 to 8. She had been in a hurry and skipped the final check.
She tests the retained sample: pH 6. The cause is clear.
She replaces the two kegs free, corrects the remaining stock to pH 7, and adds "final pH check signed before bottling" to her routine.
blocks.result: Because of her records, Amaka found the cause in minutes, kept the school's trust, and changed her process so it does not happen again.

blocks.text: Storage

items: Keep acids (sulphonic acid) and alkalis (caustic soda, soda ash) on separate shelves, with lids tight.
Store everything off the floor, out of direct sun, and locked away from children.
Keep finished products separate from raw materials, and food completely separate from both.
Use first-in, first-out: sell older batches before newer ones.

blocks.text: Waste and the environment

Detergent ingredients can harm streams, fish and wells when they arrive in concentrated form. Phosphate builders such as STPP can feed algae in rivers and lakes, which is one reason many countries have limited phosphates in detergents. Your waste will be small, but handle it with care.

items: Never pour concentrated sulphonic acid or caustic soda into drains, gutters, soil or near a well or borehole.
Leftover small amounts of acid or alkali can be slowly added to a large volume of your batch water during the next production, where they will be neutralised, or kept labelled until you can use them.
Rinse water from washing equipment is dilute; pour it into a proper drain or soakaway, away from wells.
Rinse empty chemical containers, puncture or mark them, and never give them away for storing water, oil or food.
Use only as much STPP as your tested formula needs; consider whether soda ash alone is enough where water is soft.

blocks.title: Choosing what to fix first
items: Fix now: high harm, easy
Plan: high harm, harder
Quick win: low harm, easy
Later: low harm, harder
blocks.caption: Rank your risks by harm and effort, and fix the high-harm, easy items immediately.

blocks.text: Fair and safe choices

items: Do not water down product to make more money while selling it as the same product. If you sell a cheaper, thinner grade, label and price it as such.
Do not use formalin or unknown chemicals because they are cheap.
Do not employ children to handle chemicals. Train any helper in PPE and first aid, and record that training.
Respect neighbours: mix where fumes will not blow into homes, and do not leave containers where children play.

blocks.text: Training a helper

As orders grow you may bring in a helper. Before she touches any chemical, show her the safety card, the PPE, the mixing order, the bleach rule and first aid. Let her watch one full batch, then make one under your supervision. Write the date and what you trained in your notebook and ask her to sign it. Keep an **incident log** in the same notebook: every splash, spill or near miss, what caused it and what you changed. A near miss written down today prevents an injury tomorrow.

blocks.title: Label every container in the workspace
blocks.text: Every jug, bucket and drum that holds a chemical or solution, even for an hour, should carry a label with what it is. Unlabelled caustic solution looks exactly like water. Use masking tape and a marker, and remove the label only after the container is washed.

blocks.title: One notebook, always
blocks.text: If a spreadsheet is hard, a hardcover notebook works perfectly. Use one page per batch, write in pen, and take a photo of each page on your phone as a backup.

takeaways: Every batch needs a number and a record of materials, adjustments and tests
Records let you trace complaints to their cause quickly
Store acids and alkalis apart, locked, off the floor and out of sun
Never pour concentrated chemicals into drains, soil or near wells
Never water down product secretly or reuse chemical containers for food or water

activity.title: Create your batch record template and waste plan
steps: Draw a batch record page (or spreadsheet) with all the fields listed in this lesson.
Fill it in for your most recent test batch.
Write your batch numbering system and stick it inside your notebook.
Write five lines on how you will store raw materials and handle waste and empty containers.
activity.evidence: Photo of your completed batch record page and your written storage and waste plan.

quiz.q: A batch passes pH and thickness, but the retained sample separates into layers after five days. What should you do?
options: Sell it quickly before it separates
Hold it, stir and retest, and review thickener and salt for the next batch
quiz.explain: Separation is a stability fault. Investigate the thickener and salt rather than selling a product that will fail in customers' homes.

quiz.q: A customer complains about a keg. What lets you find the cause fastest?
options: The batch number on the keg and your batch record
Asking the customer to describe it
quiz.explain: The batch number links the keg to its record and retained sample, showing materials and test results.

quiz.q: Which label claim is acceptable for a multipurpose liquid soap that has been tested on greasy plates?
options: Cuts grease on pots and plates
quiz.explain: A tested, true performance claim is fine. Germ-kill, chemical-free and doctor claims cannot be proven or are false.

quiz.q: According to NAFDAC's MSME page, how many products can be registered under micro scale?
quiz.explain: The MSME page states not more than five products can be registered under micro scale.

quiz.q: Ada has some leftover caustic soda solution after a batch. What is the responsible choice?
options: Keep it labelled and use it to neutralise in the next batch
Give it to a neighbour in a drink bottle
quiz.explain: Concentrated alkali must not go into drains or soil. Keep it labelled and use it up in production.

quiz.q: A mould spot appears in a retained sample after three weeks. What should happen to that batch?
options: Discard it and review the preservative and container cleaning
Add more perfume to hide the smell
quiz.explain: Mould means contamination. Discard, then check preservative dose and container hygiene.

modules.title: Costing, Selling and Growing Your Cleaning Products Business
modules.overview: Good product is only half a business. In this module you cost a batch to the last bottle, set retail and bulk prices that leave real profit, sell through WhatsApp, demonstrations and bulk buyers, and pull everything together into your capstone portfolio and 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Costing a batch and pricing for profit
objectives: Calculate the full cost of a batch including packaging and overheads
Work out cost per litre and per container
Set retail and bulk prices with a clear margin
Work out how many bottles you must sell to recover start-up costs

blocks.text: Many liquid soap sellers know the price of sulphonic acid but have never added up the cost of bottles, labels, transport and their own time. They feel busy but cannot find the profit. In this lesson you will cost a batch completely, then price from that number, not from what the next seller charges.

blocks.name: money-bag
blocks.caption: Profit is what is left after every cost, including packaging and transport, has been counted.

blocks.text: The four groups of cost

items: **Raw materials:** every chemical in the batch at the price you actually paid, including colour, perfume and preservative.
**Packaging:** bottles or kegs, caps, labels or stickers, and cartons or nylon for delivery.
**Overheads per batch:** transport to the market, PPE replacement, pH strips, water, a share of equipment wear, and phone data for marketing.
**Your labour:** a fair amount for your hours. If you do not count it, you cannot later afford to pay a helper.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing a 25-litre batch
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Ibadan makes 25 litres of multipurpose liquid soap. All prices are illustrative and approximate; use your own receipts.
steps: Raw materials for the batch (all chemicals, perfume, colour, preservative): 21,000 naira (approximate).
Packaging: 25 one-litre bottles with caps at 250 naira each = 6,250 naira; 25 labels at 60 naira = 1,500 naira. Total 7,750 naira.
Overheads for the batch (transport, pH strips, PPE wear, data): 3,000 naira.
Labour: 4 hours at 1,000 naira per hour = 4,000 naira.
Full batch cost: 21,000 + 7,750 + 3,000 + 4,000 = 35,750 naira. Cost per 1-litre bottle: 35,750 / 25 = 1,430 naira.
blocks.result: Grace knows each bottle costs her about 1,430 naira. Any price below that loses money, even if she is selling a lot.

blocks.text: From cost to price

Decide the **margin** you need: the share of the selling price that is profit. A simple method is **cost divided by (1 minus margin)**. For a 30% margin on a cost of 1,430 naira: 1,430 / 0.70 = about 2,043 naira, so Grace might price at 2,000 to 2,100 naira. Then compare with prices in your area. If similar quality sells for much less, look for savings in packaging or buying, not in the surfactant that does the cleaning.

blocks.text: When raw material prices rise

Chemical prices in Nigeria can change quickly, often with the exchange rate, because many raw materials are imported. Recalculate your batch cost every time you buy a new stock of raw materials. If cost rises, you have three honest choices: raise the price, change the pack size and tell customers, or accept a smaller margin for a short time. Diluting the product while keeping the same label is not an honest choice.
Break-even: how many bottles before you profit?

Your first equipment, such as drums, a scale, PPE and a stock of bottles, is a one-time **start-up cost**. To know when it is paid back, divide it by the profit you make on each bottle. For example, if Grace spent 45,000 naira (approximate) on equipment and makes about 600 naira profit on each 1-litre bottle, she needs to sell 45,000 / 600 = 75 bottles to recover her start-up money. After that, the profit is truly hers. Knowing this number helps you set a realistic sales target for your first two or three months.

Buying raw materials in larger packs is often cheaper per kilogram, but it ties up cash, and some materials, such as preservatives and perfume, have a limited shelf life. Buy bigger packs only for items you use every batch and can store safely, and only when you have regular orders to justify it.

blocks.title: Keep a one-page cost sheet
blocks.text: List every item with the price paid and the date. Update it with each purchase. A cost sheet on your phone lets you answer a bulk buyer's price request on the spot without guessing.

Finally, count only **good** containers. If two bottles leak or a batch is reworked, the cost of that loss is shared by the bottles you can actually sell. Track your losses for a few batches and include an average waste figure in your costing.

takeaways: Cost includes raw materials, packaging, overheads and your labour
Cost per container = full batch cost / number of good containers
Price = cost / (1 minus margin), then compare with the market
Break-even bottles = start-up cost / profit per bottle
Recalculate whenever raw material prices change

lessons.title: Selling: demonstrations, WhatsApp and bulk buyers
objectives: Describe your product's value with honest, specific benefits
Run a simple cleaning demonstration that wins orders
Set up WhatsApp Business with a catalogue and price list
Approach and keep bulk buyers such as restaurants and schools

blocks.text: People buy liquid soap again and again, so your real goal is not one sale but **repeat customers**. A buyer who trusts your product will order every week or month. Trust comes from three things: the product works, it is the same every time, and you deliver when you promise.

blocks.name: online-shopping
blocks.alt: A person shopping on a phone
blocks.caption: Many customers will order through WhatsApp, so your phone becomes your shop window.

blocks.text: Say what it does, specifically

"Quality liquid soap" means nothing because every seller says it. Use specific, true statements from your own tests: "Cuts palm oil grease on pots", "Thick, so a little goes far", "Near neutral pH, tested every batch", "Batch number on every bottle". Never add germ-killing or medical claims.
The demonstration

items: Bring two greasy plates or a pot with palm oil, two bowls, a measuring spoon and your product.
Measure one spoon of your product into a bowl of water. Ask the buyer to bring her current product for the second bowl.
Wash one plate in each bowl with the same number of strokes and let the buyer feel both plates.
Show your label: ingredients, warnings, batch number and your phone number.
Offer a small trial size or a first-order price, and agree a delivery day.

blocks.text: WhatsApp Business

items: Install WhatsApp Business and fill in your business profile: name, short description, location and opening hours.
Create a **catalogue** with a clear photo of each size and its price.
Use **labels** to sort chats into new customers, paid, delivered and bulk buyers.
Post on your Status two or three times a week: a fresh batch being bottled, a demo video, a happy customer's message (with permission).
Set a short greeting message and an away message so no buyer is ignored.

blocks.text: For payment, many customers prefer bank transfer or a mobile money app such as OPay or Moniepoint, and some will want a payment link from a service like Paystack. Confirm money has actually arrived in your account before you release goods, because fake transfer screenshots are a common scam.

Delivery is part of your product. Agree delivery days in advance, group deliveries by area to save transport money, and carry kegs upright with caps tight. Include the transport cost in your bulk price or charge it separately, and say which clearly on your price list.

blocks.title: Worked example: winning a restaurant account
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Abuja approaches a busy restaurant that buys keg liquid soap from the market.
steps: She asks the manager how many kegs they use: about two 25-litre kegs a month.
She does a demo on one of their oily soup pots and leaves one free 4-litre container to try for a week.
After a week she follows up; the cooks like it. She offers 25-litre kegs at her bulk price, delivered on the first Monday of each month.
She sends a written price list on WhatsApp, sets a reminder on her phone for each delivery, and asks for transfer before delivery.
blocks.result: Amaka gains a regular order of about 50 litres a month from one customer, which is easier to plan production around than many single bottles.

blocks.text: Keeping customers coming back

Getting a new customer takes far more effort than keeping one. Write down when each regular customer usually reorders and send a short, friendly message a few days before: "Good morning Madam, your monthly keg is ready for Monday delivery, should I bring it?" Keep your promise on delivery days; if you will be late, tell the customer early. When someone complains, listen, check the batch number, and fix the problem quickly, even if it costs you a free bottle.

Ask satisfied customers for a short review you can share, with their permission, and consider a simple reward for referrals, such as a free litre when a referred customer places a first order. Keep product quality exactly the same between batches; customers notice quickly when a product becomes thinner or smells different, and that is the fastest way to lose them.

blocks.title: Protect customer data
blocks.text: Keep customers' phone numbers and addresses private. Do not add people to broadcast lists or groups without asking, and never share one customer's details with another.

takeaways: Repeat orders are the heart of a cleaning products business
Use specific, tested benefits, never germ or medical claims
A side-by-side grease demo is the strongest sales tool
Set up WhatsApp Business with a catalogue, labels and regular Status posts
Confirm payment has arrived before releasing goods

lessons.title: Your capstone portfolio and 90-day plan
objectives: Assemble a complete evidence portfolio for certification
Reflect honestly on feedback and what you changed
Write a realistic 90-day production and sales plan
Check your work against the certification checklist

blocks.text: This final lesson brings together everything you have done. Your capstone is a **portfolio**: a folder of evidence showing that you can make a safe, consistent cleaning product, test it, label it honestly, cost it and sell it. It is also the starting file you will show to a NAFDAC officer, a bank, a cooperative or a bulk buyer who asks how you work.

blocks.name: certificate
blocks.caption: Your certificate is earned by real evidence: a safe batch, tested, recorded, costed and sold.

blocks.text: What goes in your portfolio

items: Your safety station photos and safety card (Module 1).
Your raw materials sheet with real chemical names, strengths and suppliers.
Your master formula written per litre, with test batch records that led to it (Module 2).
One full production batch record with pH, flow time, grease test and stability check (Module 3).
Your specification and a photo of your retained sample.
Your honest label and NAFDAC readiness checklist.
Your cost sheet and prices (Module 4).
Evidence of at least two customers or testers using the product, and their feedback.
A short reflection and your 90-day plan.

blocks.text: Writing an honest reflection

A good reflection is short and specific. Answer four questions: What did I make? What went wrong, and how did I find out? What did I change? What will I do differently next time? "My third batch stung hands because I skipped the final pH check; I now sign the pH reading before bottling" is far stronger than "I learnt a lot".
Your 90-day plan

blocks.title: A 90-day plan
items: Days 1-30: steady batches

blocks.caption: Each month builds on the last: first consistency, then customers, then formal growth.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting realistic targets
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kaduna has made three good batches of 25 litres and sells about 30 litres a month to neighbours.
steps: She sets a target of two regular restaurant accounts by day 60, each taking about 50 litres a month.
That would raise her sales to about 30 + 100 = 130 litres a month, so she plans about five 25-litre batches a month by day 90.
Using her cost sheet, she checks she has enough money to buy raw materials for two batches at once, and asks restaurants to pay on delivery.
She writes one review date at the end of each month to compare actual sales with her plan.
blocks.result: Halima's plan is tied to real buyers, real production capacity and real cash, so she can see each month whether she is on track.

blocks.text: Choosing your next product

Add a second product only when your first one meets its specification batch after batch and you have regular buyers. Good next steps build on what you already know: a liquid hand wash using SLES, or a laundry liquid, both made with similar equipment and the same testing routine. Remember NAFDAC's micro-scale limit of five products and plan which ones matter most to your buyers. Avoid jumping to bleach or germ-killing products; they carry higher chemical risk and need approval you would have to plan for carefully.

Look for support around you: an experienced producer who will let you watch a batch, a women's cooperative or savings group that can help with bulk buying, and your local NAFDAC office for questions about registration. Bring your portfolio to these conversations. It shows that you work safely and keep records, and it makes people more willing to help, buy from or lend to you.

blocks.title: Keep your evidence organised
blocks.text: Create one folder on your phone or in Google Drive named with your business name and the course. Inside, make a sub-folder for each module. Name photos clearly, for example "batch LS-2611-03 pH test".
Certification checklist

items: I can explain and follow the safe mixing order and the bleach rule.
I have a master formula with test records that support it.
I have made and fully recorded at least one production batch that met my specification.
My label is honest, with warnings, batch number and no germ or medical claims.
I know my cost per container and my selling prices.
I have real feedback from at least two users and a written reflection.
I have a 90-day plan with dates and numbers.

blocks.text: When every line is true, submit your portfolio, then take the final quiz. You need at least 70% in the final quiz and a completed practical capstone to receive your certificate.

takeaways: Your portfolio is proof of safe, consistent, honest production
Reflections should name what went wrong and what you changed
A 90-day plan links production to real buyers and cash
Add a second product only when the first is consistent
Certification needs the capstone plus at least 70% in the final quiz
